title: Micro-Mobility Services
desc: Plan and run a small shared bike or scooter service: fleet, safety, parking, pricing, maintenance and city rules.
outcomes: Explain micro-mobility types and where they fit.
Plan fleet size, zones and parking.
task: Plan a 30-day pilot of a shared micro-mobility service for one campus or district, with fleet, safety rules, maintenance, pricing and a community plan.
condition: A computer, a map, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. Real vehicles are not required.
standard: Fleet and cost maths correct; safety rules and rider age limits stated; parking and permits checked; maintenance plan has daily checks; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Campus managers, tourism staff, city assistants, entrepreneurs.
evidence: zone map, fleet sheet, safety rules, price sheet, maintenance plan
modules: Types and fit
Understand
Different vehicles suit different places.
Bikes, e-bikes, scooters and cargo bikes have different range, speed and cost.
Short trips under 5 km are the main use.
E-assist helps on hills and with longer trips.
Match to local roads, weather and rules.
Look at local street width, slopes and weather before choosing vehicles.
E-bikes need secure charging; scooters have higher injury risk at speed.
A hilly campus picks e-bikes because they allow fast trips up slopes without sweat. A flat tourist promenade suits light bikes; a hilly university suits e-bikes with 60 km range.
Compare three vehicle types in a table. Add a site-fit note.
Table includes range, cost and best use.
Zones and parking
Apply
Order on the street keeps the service welcome.
Pick start points near demand.
Marked parking, no-go zones and speed limits.
Work with the owner or authority.
Review complaints.
Place parking where people already walk, such as gates, stations and shops.
Use geofencing in the app to slow vehicles in busy zones or end trips only in bays.
Parking bays at gates reduce clutter; a no-go zone near a hospital entrance prevents blocked access. A campus limits scooters to 10 km/h in the library courtyard through the app.
Draw a zone map for a campus or district. Mark slow zones on your map.
Zones are marked and justified.
Fleet sizing and rebalancing
Analyse
Not too many and not too few.
Fleet = peak trips / trips per vehicle per day.
Rebalancing moves vehicles from places where they pile up to where they are needed.
Start small and measure.
Keep spares for repair.
Use trip data to adjust fleet weekly; shift vehicles before peak hours.
Keep 15 to 20 per cent of the fleet under repair or charging.
60 peak trips at 6 trips per vehicle need 10 vehicles plus 2 spares. With 12 vehicles and 20 per cent unavailable, only about 10 are on the street at any time.
Size a fleet for your case. Add a repair buffer to your sizing.
Maths correct.
Rider safety
Evaluate
Prevent injuries.
Helmets, lights, speed limits and age limits.
Rider tips and clear rules in the app.
Incident log and insurance.
Safe parking and pedestrian priority.
Offer a short in-app safety quiz before the first ride.
Record injuries and near misses and share lessons weekly.
A slow-speed zone is set near pedestrians and the speed is limited remotely. After a quiz is added, near misses fall by a third in a month.
Write safety rules. Write a first-ride safety quiz of five questions.
Rules measurable.
Maintenance and charging
Apply
Safe vehicles every day.
Daily check: brakes, tyres, lights, bell and lock.
Battery swaps and safe charging.
Spare parts and tools.
Log every repair.
Replace worn tyres and brake pads on a schedule, not only on failure.
Train staff to handle batteries; never charge damaged packs.
A tag shows last check date; vehicles failing a check are removed. A weekly brake and tyre check finds three worn pads before any incident.
Create a check card. Create a weekly maintenance calendar.
Card has ten items.
Pricing and money
Evaluate
Cover costs and stay fair.
Unlock fee plus per-minute price; passes.
Costs: vehicles, staff, charging, repair, insurance and permits.
Break-even trips per day.
Discounts for students and low-income riders.
Offer a student day pass and a low-income discount to widen access.
Track revenue per vehicle per day against cost per vehicle.
Break-even is 4.2 trips per vehicle per day at a 20 INR average fare. Revenue of 90 INR per vehicle-day against a cost of 70 INR gives 20 INR margin.
Build a pricing sheet. Test two price levels with a mock demand.
Currency shown.
Community and environment
Evaluate
Be a good neighbour.
Noise, sidewalk clutter and accessibility.
Complaint line and response times.
Recycling of batteries and parts.
Local jobs.
Publish a contact number and respond to complaints in 24 hours.
Offer vehicle adaptations for riders with disabilities where possible.
A fine for blocking paths is explained in rules and enforced fairly. A trike option and a pickup service help riders who cannot use a scooter.
List community actions. Write a response plan.
Each has an owner.
Pilot plan
Create
Test before scaling.
Targets for trips, safety and complaints.
Review weekly.
Decide to stop, change or grow.
Share results.
Define stop rules: stop the pilot if serious injuries occur.
Report to the authority and community monthly.
The pilot adds two bays after complaints and raises utilisation. The pilot is paused after two incidents to review rules and then resumed with stricter zones.
Present the plan. Define your stop rules.
Peers can follow.
quiz: Typical trip length?
Under about 5 km. (Covered in module 1: Types and fit. To pass that module: Table includes range, cost and best use.)
Fleet formula?
Peak trips / trips per vehicle per day. (Covered in module 2: Zones and parking. To pass that module: Zones are marked and justified.)
Name a safety rule.
Helmets or speed limits. (Covered in module 3: Fleet sizing and rebalancing. To pass that module: Maths correct.)
Daily check items?
Brakes, tyres, lights, bell, lock. (Covered in module 4: Rider safety. To pass that module: Rules measurable.)
Break-even idea?
Trips per day needed to cover costs. (Covered in module 5: Maintenance and charging. To pass that module: Card has ten items.)
Why parking zones?
To avoid clutter. (Covered in module 6: Pricing and money. To pass that module: Currency shown.)
Why insurance?
Covers incidents. (Covered in module 7: Community and environment. To pass that module: Each has an owner.)
What is rebalancing?
Moving vehicles to demand. (Covered in module 8: Pilot plan. To pass that module: Peers can follow.)
Name a community issue.
Noise or blocked paths. (Covered in module 8: Pilot plan. To pass that module: Peers can follow.)
What is a pilot?
A short test before scaling. (Covered in module 8: Pilot plan. To pass that module: Peers can follow.)
